common_name: Renaissance Vanhoutte Spirea (Disease-Resistant Improved Bridal Wreath Spirea)

planting.note: Plant container or bare-root shrubs in early spring or fall in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; prune only immediately after flowering, since flower buds for the following year form on the current season's wood.

directions: Renaissance was selected as a cleaner-foliaged improvement on the classic Vanhoutte spirea, bred to resist the powdery mildew and leaf spot that often disfigure the species by midsummer, so the arching mound of blue-green leaves stays presentable all season. In late spring the long, gracefully arching branches disappear under dense clusters of small white flowers lining the stems, repeating the old-fashioned bridal-wreath look on a plant that holds its foliage quality longer into the growing season. Fall brings a bonus of orange-red leaf color that the plain species rarely provides. Prune only right after the spring bloom finishes, removing a portion of the oldest canes at ground level every few years to keep the naturally large, fountain-like shrub from becoming congested at the base.

common_name: Pink Ice Vanhoutte Spirea (Variegated Pink-and-Cream New-Growth Spirea)

planting.note: Plant in moist, well-drained soil in full sun for the strongest variegation, since shaded growth tends toward plain green; prune immediately after flowering and remove any shoots that revert fully to green as soon as they appear.

directions: Pink Ice was selected by English nurseryman Peter Catt for foliage rather than flowers, opening each new shoot in salmon-pink and cream mottling on red stems before the leaves mature to a quieter green-and-cream variegation as summer progresses. Clusters of small white flowers still appear along the arching branches in spring in the familiar bridal-wreath style, but the real display is the repeated flush of pink-tinted new growth through the season. It grows noticeably slower and stays considerably smaller and denser than the plain species, making it useful where a full-size Vanhoutte spirea would overwhelm the space. Because variegated shoots occasionally revert to solid green, cut reverted branches out promptly so they don't outcompete the patterned growth.

common_name: Double Play Red Spirea (Red-New-Growth Compact Spirea with Crimson-Pink Blooms)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in average, well-drained soil in full sun to part sun; the mounded habit needs no regular pruning or shearing to look tidy.

directions: Double Play Red opens its season with new leaves glowing bright red, a sharper and more saturated color than the orange-red flush typical of older spirea cultivars, before the foliage settles into a cool burgundy-tinged green for summer. Rounded clusters of deep crimson-pink flowers cover the compact mound in late spring into early summer, drawing butterflies and hummingbirds, and because the cultivar is sterile it will not seed into surrounding beds the way some older spireas can. Its naturally neat, mounded form holds its shape without shearing, making it a low-maintenance choice for foundation plantings or mixed borders where a tidy small shrub is wanted. It tolerates heat, average soil, and dry spells once established, and shows good resistance to the deer browsing and foliar disease that trouble some other spirea selections.
